facts: The guide shows how to publish snapshot builds and delete them from the registry and the index. [L9]
Leftover snapshot tags fill the registry, and a deleted release cannot be undone. [L11]
The prune command deletes registry tags, but only tags the index marks as ephemeral. [L13]
The announce command is the only command that writes the index, and it removes rows for tags the registry no longer has. [L13]
A track is one pre-release line whose builds are build-numbered tags, with a rolling tag pointing at the newest build. [L15]
Each snapshot is pushed with a fixed-width build id and without a keep tag. [L19]
The canary push example uses cascade, no keep tag, a datetime build id and a shared tags file. [L21]
A datetime build timestamp appends an underscore and a YYYYMMDDhhmmss stamp to the tag. [L26]
Cascade stays inside its own pre-release, so 0.5, 0 and latest never move. [L26]
The tags file receives the pushed tag and the rolling tag, one per line. [L26]
Ephemeral builds need the no-keep-tag flag, otherwise prune frees no storage. [L29]
Each push writes a keep tag per platform manifest by default, and that protection defeats prune. [L31]
A leftover keep tag keeps manifests and layers reachable, so registry garbage collection never reclaims them. [L34]
Neither prune nor announce checks for keep tags, so the failure is silent and the registry keeps growing. [L34]
The keep-builds ordering compares build segments as text, so build ids must have equal width. [L38]
A date-only build timestamp is not fixed-width: two builds on one day share a tag and the second overwrites the first. [L40]
A canary is rebuilt on every commit, and only the newest few builds are kept. [L44]
The canary pipeline pushes, prunes, repairs rolling tags and announces in one index update. [L44]
The canary recipe runs four commands on one tags file and prunes down to one build. [L46]
PKG is the package name as the index records it. [L57]
REG is the registry repository the tags live in. [L58]
FORGE names the index repository and the forge type that announce talks to. [L58]
Announce reads the committed index entry even when its output goes to a local directory. [L61]
Prune deletes every older canary build listed in the index, keeping the newest build and the rolling tag. [L63]
Cascade repair moves nothing in the canary recipe; it matters only when prune deletes a rolling tag's source. [L65]
Announce adds the new build as an ephemeral row, refreshes the rolling row and removes rows of deleted builds. [L65]
Without a pipeline, the output flag writes the rebuilt index entry locally; in CI, dropping it opens a request instead. [L68]
The ephemeral flag marks only rows a run adds and never changes an existing row. [L70]
Prune deletes only tags the served index lists as ephemeral, so the first run of a new track deletes nothing. [L72]
A change request gets its own track, and teardown prunes every build of it plus the rolling tag. [L76]
Teardown leaves the latest, 0.5 and 0 tags untouched. [L84]
Rerunning a teardown is safe: pruning an empty registry exits 0 with an empty tags file. [L90]
Announce given an empty tags file exits 0 and changes nothing, before any forge or registry work. [L99]
The refresh announce removes each ephemeral row whose tag is gone from the registry. [L99]
An explicit tag list may delete any tag, including tags outside snapshot tracks. [L105]
With lazy sync, the teardown job only prunes and a scheduled job converges the index. [L112]
Never schedule the tags-from-registry option, because it makes unannounced snapshots durable and prune then refuses them with exit 81. [L119]
Prune checks every selected tag against the served index root before its first delete. [L123]
Tags listed with the ephemeral marker are deleted. [L127]
Tags listed without the marker make prune exit 81 and delete nothing. [L128]
Tags missing from the index but present in the registry make prune exit 75 and delete nothing. [L129]
Tags neither listed nor present in the registry are reported as absent. [L130]
Exit 81 protects releases; the force flag deletes such tags anyway, and the index row stays until a reviewed announce. [L132]
Without an index to consult, prune also exits 81 until the force flag is passed. [L132]
Exit 75 usually means the build's announce has not merged yet, so retry later. [L134]
A dry run applies the same check, exits the same way and deletes nothing. [L134]
A push that succeeded without a matching announce leaves a build the index does not list, so prunes exit 75. [L138]
To recover, append the orphaned tag to the tags file and announce it as an ephemeral row. [L140]
Prune never announces, and splitting push and announce into separate jobs stops a retry from pushing twice. [L147]
Build tags are unique so builds cannot race, but the rolling tag can. [L151]
Run one track's jobs one at a time using GitLab resource groups or GitHub concurrency groups. [L153]
Both CI examples split push from announce, so a retried announce reuses the pushed tags file. [L157]
Registry credentials need push and delete rights, and the index credential is the announce token variable. [L157]
Retry only exit 75; never retry exit 69 or 82. [L159]
The GitLab canary push job runs only on the default branch, inside a resource group. [L173]
The GitLab canary publish job prunes down to ten builds and retries on exit 75. [L185]
The GitLab merge-request push publishes a per-request tag and an environment that auto-stops after three days. [L190]
A manual GitLab teardown job prunes and announces the merge-request track. [L206]
A scheduled GitLab job runs announce with refresh to converge the index. [L217]
The environment on_stop hook runs the teardown when the merge request closes. [L223]
The GitHub workflow runs on pull request events and on a daily cron schedule. [L227]
The GitHub concurrency group is per pull request and does not cancel in-progress runs. [L232]
The GitHub push job skips closed pull requests and passes its tags to the announce job as output. [L242]
The GitHub teardown job runs when the pull request is closed. [L266]
The examples omit registry login, so use the credential variables instead. [L287]
Prune needs a registry that deletes tags, which the OCI distribution spec makes optional. [L291]
A registry that refuses deletion fails the first delete with exit 82 and deletes nothing. [L291]
zot v2.1.18 answers 202 and removes the tag, so prune works. [L297]
registry:2 with delete disabled answers 405, and prune exits 82. [L298]
registry:2 with delete enabled answers 400 DIGEST_INVALID, the tag stays, and prune exits 82. [L299]
GHCR, Docker Hub and Amazon ECR offer no tag deletion through their APIs, so prune exits 82 there, per their docs, untested here. [L301]
Exit 82 is never transient, so do not retry it. [L303]
Announce cannot clean up an emptied repository that some registries drop; it exits 79 and removes nothing. [L307]
zot and registry:2 keep a repository after its last tag. [L307]
Prune deletes tags only, never content; registry garbage collection reclaims the storage. [L308]
Prune never writes the index; removals reach it only through announce. [L309]
